description.p: Before the Severing, the Seramai lived among canopy bridges, cliff settlements, and wind-carved stone — places most others considered too exposed, too high, or too precarious to call home.
To the Seramai, height was never danger. It was clarity.

They built no empires and claimed no thrones. Their settlements were small and deliberate, tucked into the edges of the world where they could see clearly and move freely. They traded with neighboring peoples, raised families in narrow perches above busy cities, and filled roles that rewarded agility and quiet — scouts, guides, messengers, and the occasional thief.

Seramai rarely claim territory — but they remember places. A rooftop, a beam, a narrow path along a wall. These become part of their mental map of the world, returned to years later as if no time had passed.
They have never ruled the continent. They have never needed to.
When the Severing shattered the old world, the Seramai adapted the way they always had — by finding the high ground and waiting to see what settled.

Canopy bridges collapsed. Cliff settlements crumbled. But the instinct that built them survived intact. In the fractured cities and broken towers of the new world, the Seramai simply found new perches. Rooftops replaced canopies. Ruined spires replaced carved stone.

They were present in Atérior before the Severing, and they are present still — never dominant, never erased. In a world fractured by ruin and instability, the Seramai endure not by conquering, but by creating spaces of calm wherever they settle.
Among the Seramai, safety is not a structure. It is a presence. A place becomes safe not when it is secured, but when it is shared with those they trust.
They build nests, not forts. And somehow, that has always been enough.

Seramai rarely gather in massive caravans or centralized nations. Instead they organize in small clan-circles — a couple, their children, perhaps grandparents or a closely trusted friend. They integrate into cities and settlements without overwhelming them.

They gravitate toward professions that reward independence and mobility: scouts, couriers, treasure hunters, performers, rangers, monks, fighters, and guides. They do not avoid society — they simply move through it lightly.

Seramai are fully furred humanoids with distinctly feline anatomy. Their builds tend toward lean, long-limbed frames designed for agility and controlled bursts of motion. They walk digitigrade, balanced on the balls of their feet rather than flat-footed.

Fur coloration varies widely — from tabby and mottled housecat patterns to sleek panther-black, snow-pale coats, spotted leopard patterns, or deep desert tones. Facial structure ranges from pronounced muzzles to subtler feline contours, but they are always unmistakably catlike.

Most Seramai possess tails, though length and thickness vary. It is common for Seramai children to purr frequently — in adulthood it becomes a personal habit rather than a reflex, surfacing most often in moments of genuine comfort or trust.
Your Seramai character has the following racial traits.

Creature Type. Humanoid.
Size. Small or Medium (chosen at character creation).
Speed. Your base walking speed is 30 feet. You have a climbing speed equal to your walking speed.
Ability Score Increase. Increase one ability score by 2 and a different ability score by 1, or increase three different ability scores by 1.
Darkvision. Accustomed to twilight movement and low-light environments, you can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You discern only shades of gray in darkness.
Feline Claws. Your claws are natural weapons, which you can use to make unarmed strikes. On a hit, they deal 1d6 + your Strength modifier slashing damage instead of bludgeoning damage.
Silent Perception. You have proficiency in Perception. Your natural stillness and instinct for elevation work in your favor — when you are in dim light, on high ground, or climbing, you have advantage on Stealth checks.
Sure-Footed Descent. Your body is built for balance and controlled impact. When you fall, reduce the effective distance of the fall by a number of feet equal to 5 × your proficiency bonus. You land on your feet unless you are incapacitated.
Languages. You can speak, read, and write Common and one other language of your choice.
Seramai are a familiar presence in almost every major settlement — not because they gather in large numbers, but because they have a talent for being exactly where they are needed.

They fill the spaces others overlook. The courier who knows every rooftop shortcut. The scout who was already in position before the order was given. The guide who moves through ruins like they were built for her specifically.

In adventuring parties, Seramai tend to operate at the edges — not out of distrust, but out of habit. They read the room before they enter it. They find the exits before they find the seats. This can read as caution or as coldness, depending on who is watching.
Those who know them understand it differently. A Seramai who stays is not someone who failed to leave. They are someone who decided you were worth remaining for.
Among the Seramai, purring is not discussed openly.

It simply happens — or it doesn't. In childhood it is constant and uncontrolled, a reflex of comfort and safety. In adulthood it becomes something quieter and rarer, surfacing only when the body decides, without consultation, that it is safe.
Outsiders who hear it for the first time often do not know what to say.
Most Seramai prefer it that way.
You are Small. Your build is lighter and more compact, suited to tight perches and narrow ledges.
You are Medium. Your build is leaner and longer-limbed than a typical Small Seramai, favoring reach and speed.

Accustomed to twilight movement and low-light environments, you can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You discern only shades of gray in darkness.
